abstract: Open-vocabulary segmentation (OVS) enables models to segment a variety of concepts specified in natural language, removing the need for fixed label sets and fine-tuning. While recent OVS approaches have shown strong performance on natural images, they transfer poorly to Earth observation (EO) data due to differing semantics, scales, sensing modality, and geographic context. To date, large-scale EO-specific datasets and benchmarks for OVS remain scarce. We, therefore, introduce TerraMesh-Masks, a large-scale open-vocabulary segmentation dataset for EO, comprising 16 million binary masks aligned with nine million multimodal TerraMesh samples and annotated using OpenStreetMap and Overture-derived semantics. In addition, we provide an expert-reviewed evaluation set of 523 samples covering over 200 classes to enable robust evaluation. To demonstrate the impact of TerraMesh-Masks, we build an open-vocabulary version of TerraMind. Our results demonstrate significantly improved performance over general-purpose state-of-the-art models reaching 35.18% IoU versus 16.29% for DINOv3.txt and 11.33% for SAM-3. We release the dataset publicly under a permissive license at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibm-esa-geospatial/TerraMesh-Masks.

sections.body: The section motivates open-vocabulary segmentation (OVS) for Earth observation (EO) data, arguing that models built for natural images transfer poorly to satellite imagery. It lists three contributions: TerraMesh-Masks, a dataset of 16 million image-mask samples built on TerraMesh; TerraMesh-Masks-Eval, an expert-reviewed evaluation set; and TerraMind-OVS, an open-vocabulary extension of TerraMind. The authors report that TerraMind-OVS outperforms SAM-3 and DINOv3.txt, and many EO-specific models such as GeoPixel, in the vast majority of categories, as shown in Fig. 1.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Open-vocabulary segmentation lacks large satellite datasets and benchmarks, which the paper addresses with TerraMesh-Masks and an evaluation set.

sections.body: The section groups prior work into general vision-language models, such as CLIP, and their segmentation extensions, including CAT-Seg, SAN, SAM-3, and DINOv3.txt. It then reviews Earth observation adaptations: training-free methods such as SegEarth-OV and DINO Soars, and fine-tuned models such as OVRSISS and AerOSeg trained on high-resolution aerial datasets. Table 1 compares datasets. TerraMesh-Masks has 9M images, a vocabulary size of 44k, S1, S2, RGB, and DEM modalities, 10m resolution, and an ODbL license. The authors note that other datasets focus on high-resolution imagery or cover a limited set of semantic classes, and that some listed licenses may not reflect source restrictions.
sections.heading: Related work
sections.headline: Existing remote-sensing open-vocabulary datasets mostly use high-resolution imagery and cover few semantic classes.

sections.body: Candidate masks start from OpenStreetMap and Overture Maps tags, filtered against TerraMesh patches, from roughly 93 million raw candidates. Heuristics then remove 43.5 million candidates (46.4%) and sample up to three masks per image, leaving 20.17 million for a large language model. Mistral-Large-3 scores each mask for visual coherence and proposes a class label and synonyms. Masks scoring above 0.5 are kept, giving 16.07 million accepted, an acceptance rate of 79.7%. The result covers more than 44,000 unique class labels and over 537,000 synonym strings. The authors state that Overture annotations can be imprecise and that the OpenStreetMap schema is noisy.
sections.heading: TerraMesh-Masks
sections.headline: TerraMesh-Masks adds roughly 16 million language-labelled masks to nine million TerraMesh patches, built from OpenStreetMap and Overture Maps.

sections.body: TerraMind-OVS keeps the TerraMind encoder-decoder and changes little, so that gains can be attributed to TerraMesh-Masks. The class query is encoded by a CLIP text encoder (OpenAI ViT-B-32), projected by a two-layer MLP with GELU activation and hidden size 1024, and converted into five learned query tokens. The decoder predicts 196 mask tokens on a 14×14 grid. A separately trained binary-mask tokenizer converts masks to and from pixels, following TerraMind's Land-Use-Land-Cover tokenizer. Training uses cross-entropy on the target mask tokens, and the mask is added as a modality through continuous pretraining.
sections.heading: TerraMind-OVS
sections.headline: TerraMind-OVS treats binary masks as an extra modality, predicting mask tokens conditioned on a text query.

sections.body: Training uses TerraMesh-Masks samples in a filtered WebDataset pipeline, with class-dependent repeat-factor resampling and removal of masks with invalid geometry. Images are cropped to 224×224 pixels with patch size 16. Two variants are trained: one with all modalities and one limited to S2 L2A and RGB. Text queries use the main label, sampled with factor 3 relative to synonyms, and MS-CLIP prompt templates. TerraMind-OVS-S uses batch size 1024 and learning rate 5e-4. Base and large use 512 and 1e-4, with AdamW and cosine decay. Evaluation passes full 256×256 images without resizing. SAM-3 uses confidence threshold 0.1 and RemoteSAM uses 0.5. TerraMind-OVS-L training required around 250 NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU hours.
sections.heading: Experimental setup
sections.headline: TerraMind small, base, and large are continually pretrained on TerraMesh-Masks for 15B tokens, 3% of original training.

sections.body: Table 2 reports averages over 523 evaluation samples with Student-t 95% confidence intervals. TerraMind-OVS-L improves on SAM-3 by 479% and on DINOv3.txt by 53% in relative mIoU. Among EO-specific baselines, SegEarth-OV has the best IoUpos at 21.59%, and TerraMind-OVS-L still improves on it by 13.59pp IoUpos. GeoPixel has the second-best mIoU, 14.29pp below TerraMind. The authors note that most baselines overpredict, which also results in high average recall. TerraMind-OVS takes between 52 and 73 ms per sample, while GeoPixel takes 6,298 ms on a single A100.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: TerraMind-OVS reaches 35.18% IoU against 16.29% for DINOv3.txt, the strongest generalist baseline.

sections.body: The vocabulary covers persistent map features, so dynamic phenomena such as clouds, floods, fire, or seasonal change are absent. A model trained only on this dataset cannot segment them. Automatic annotation introduces wrong labels and imprecise boundaries, and filtering reduces but does not eliminate them. Coverage follows OpenStreetMap density: 13 of the 523 evaluation samples lie above 60°, and none are in Antarctica. The 523-sample set gives wide 95% intervals, which makes distinguishing TerraMind-OVS variants difficult, and per-group results rest on as few as ten samples. The authors say the benchmark is reliable for large differences between model families but should not rank closely matched checkpoints.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Limits are a static vocabulary, noisy automatic labels, bias toward Europe and North America, and a small evaluation set.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the gap in open-vocabulary segmentation for Earth observation and the two main contributions. These are TerraMesh-Masks, a large-scale multimodal dataset, and TerraMind-OVS, an extension of TerraMind that shows performance gains from the dataset. The authors hope the dataset, benchmarks, and baselines enable broader adoption and future research in this field. The section gives no new numbers or experiments; those appear in earlier sections.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The authors conclude that the dataset and baselines could support scalable, modality-aware open-vocabulary segmentation in Earth observation.

sections.body: The acknowledgments name the FAST-EO – CCN2 project as the funding source, supported by the European Space Agency (ESA) Φ-Lab under contract number 4000143501/23/I-DT. The section does not describe methods, data, or results. Its only content is this funding statement, which identifies the project and the contract under which the work was supported. No other details about the research, its team, or its outputs appear in this section.
sections.heading: Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding

sections.body: The appendix describes TerraMesh, with 264×264 pixel patches and 17 TB of shuffled WebDataset archives, and says TerraMesh-Masks requires an additional 1.2 TB. It breaks down the evaluation set: 83 countries, with 126 samples in North America, 101 in Europe, and 23 in Africa, and 13 samples above 60° latitude. Table 4 groups the samples into 14 label groups, from inland water to recreation. It gives the annotation prompt, quality scores, and heuristics for frequency, NDVI-based spectral quality, and class downsampling. Pretraining also keeps only masks with an NDVI agreement score of at least 0.4, which removes roughly 23% of released training masks. A mask-size analysis shows TerraMind-OVS-L (S2) rising from 6.6% IoUpos on the smallest bin to 76.9% on the largest. A CaFFe case study finds that strong distribution shifts limit generalizability.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists TerraMesh details, dataset statistics, large language model prompts, filtering, training, and extra analyses.
